explains: A formation is the shape a unit stands in, and shape is not decoration — it is arithmetic. Two things come straight out of it: FRONTAGE, how many men can physically reach the enemy; and DENSITY, how many men stand in a square metre, which is the only thing arrows care about. Every formation is a bet — strong against one thing because it chose to be weak against another — and the commander's craft is making the enemy's bets wrong.

fields.manWidthMm: How much frontage each man takes. Together with the rank depth this is what turns a number of men into a shape on the ground with a real width and a real flank.
fields.rankDepthMm: How much depth each rank takes. Deep formations are narrow, which is exactly the trade: hard to break through, easy to walk around.
fields.speedMulPermille: Movement speed in thousandths. A tight formation moves slowly because keeping the line is what is slowing it down.
fields.roadSpeedMulPermille: Movement speed along a road, in thousandths. Column is transport, not a fighting shape, and this is why you use it.
fields.cohesionCapPermille: The highest cohesion this formation permits, in thousandths. Loose order cannot be neat — that is what makes it loose.
fields.changeTicks: How long the unit takes to change into this formation. Time spent changing is time spent being neither one thing nor the other, and it is when units get caught.
fields.missileDensityPermille: How good a target the formation makes, in thousandths. Packed men are easier to hit, which is the standing argument against close order under archery.
fields.shockDeliveredMulPermille: How much of a charge's force this formation delivers. Concentrated shapes hit harder because the weight arrives in one place.
fields.shockReceivedMulPermille: How much of an incoming charge lands. A shape built to absorb shock spreads the blow over more men.
fields.shockResistBonus: Flat resistance to being shocked, on top of the multiplier. Some shapes simply do not come apart when hit.
fields.shockConcentrationMulPermille: How much the formation focuses its charge onto a narrow point rather than spreading it along a face.
fields.frontShieldMulPermille: How much more the shields are worth to the front in this formation — a shieldwall is shields overlapping, and this is that.
fields.frontageMulPermille: How much wider or narrower the shape stands than its men would naturally occupy.
fields.refusalMulPermille: How much this formation multiplies the refusal a braced unit projects. A neat line refuses horses; a ragged one does not.
fields.allArcBrace: Whether bracing works in every direction rather than only to the front. Rare, expensive to form, and the answer to being surrounded.
fields.targetRanksDefault: How many ranks are engaged and fighting by default. Men in the ranks behind these are present but not swinging.
fields.targetFiles: How many files across are engaged. With the rank count, this decides how many men are actually in the fight rather than merely in the unit.
fields.requires: What a unit must have or be to adopt this shape at all. Not every formation is available to everybody.
fields.shape: The geometric arrangement, named. A description for the reader, not a number the engine reads.

geometry.explains: A hundred men in five ranks are twenty men wide; in ten ranks, ten wide. The first can fight twenty at a time; the second has five extra rows to feed forward when the front rank dies. Wide kills faster; deep lasts longer. There is no right answer, which is why it is a choice.

formations.name: Close Order
formations.explains: Shoulder to shoulder, each man owning about two-thirds of a square metre. Everything to do with pushing, holding and receiving a charge wants this. Everything to do with not being shot hates it — close order takes three and a half times the arrows loose order does.

formations.name: Open Order
formations.explains: Spread out with room to move. Arrows mostly go past. So does everything else you might want to do to somebody: you cannot push, cannot hold a line, and can neither deliver nor absorb a charge. Open order is for people who intend not to be there when the fighting happens.
formations.readOnField: You can count the gaps between men from across the field.

formations.name: Shield Wall
formations.explains: Tighter than close order, shields overlapping so each man is partly covered by his neighbour's. Front shield up by a quarter, shock resistance up, speed down to a crawl — and it is the densest arrow target on the field. The trap: overlap only works while the line HOLDS. Below 300,000 cohesion the shield bonus halves, because the wall has stopped being a wall.
formations.readOnField: Shields visibly overlapping, and the whole thing moving at a crawl.

formations.name: Wedge
formations.explains: Cavalry in a blunt arrowhead: half the frontage, so half as many men can fight — but the shock of the charge is concentrated into the point and multiplied by 1.7. A wedge is a chisel: it punches a hole in one specific place. Once the charge is spent, the same narrow front means very few of your riders can actually swing at anybody — and if the point stops on braced points, the whole wedge piles up behind it.
formations.readOnField: A visible point at the front of the horsemen, and the hole it makes.

formations.name: Column of March
formations.explains: Four men wide and long as a road — the shape armies move in, never the shape they fight in. On a road it is half again as fast. It is also helpless: only four men can fight, and a column caught in contact has no front at all — everything lands as a flank. Reinforcements arrive in column, and buying them the eight-plus seconds to shake out of it is your problem.
formations.readOnField: A long snake. If it is still a snake when the enemy arrives, somebody has made a serious mistake.

formations.name: Ring of Points
formations.explains: A ring of pikemen, points outward all the way round. It solves the pike block's one fatal weakness — that bracing is front-arc only — by having no flanks and no rear at all. Cavalry cannot touch it from any direction. And it cannot move. At all. Ever. So it becomes the densest, most obliging arrow target that has ever existed, standing perfectly still. The correct answer to being surrounded by horsemen, and the worst possible answer to anything else.
formations.readOnField: A hedgehog. Beautiful, motionless, and doomed if the enemy has bows.

formations.name: Skirmish Screen
formations.explains: Barely a formation: men scattered with two metres between them. Arrows essentially do not work on these people — nor does anything they might try to do to somebody, which is fine, because their job is to be a nuisance and go home.
